title: A ferry operator's dry-dock overrides

blocks.text: A ferry operator schedules each vessel's dry-dock overhaul in one of the years 2027 to 2031. The model in `docks.py` has a binary `x[vid, t]` for each vessel and each year `t` in its `years`, and each vessel docks at most once (given). The fleet managers send three kinds of override, each a tuple:

items: `("lock", vid, year)`: the vessel docks in `year`, and in no other year. If `year` is not one of the vessel's `years`, the lock cannot be kept, and the vessel does not dock in this plan at all: the reference closes every year the vessel has, as for a ban, and the model stays solvable.
`("ban", vid)`: the vessel does not dock in this plan.
`("by", vid, year)`: if the vessel docks, it docks in `year` or earlier.

`apply_overrides(x, vessels, overrides)` changes the model so that it allows exactly the plans that keep every override, **using only the variables' bounds** (no rows), and returns a record of what it changed.
`undo_overrides(changes)` takes that record and puts every bound back exactly as it was before `apply_overrides`, even a bound that was not 0 or 1 at the time.

blocks.text: Write down, for each kind of override, which variables' bounds it sets and to what, before you code it. Then decide what `undo_overrides` needs to know about each change, and make your record hold it.
The tests fix plans through the remaining bounds and ask the solver whether the model accepts them, and they read the bounds back after an undo. About fifteen lines.

from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass

from ortools.math_opt.python import mathopt


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Vessel:
    vid: str
    years: tuple[int, ...]


def apply_overrides(x: dict, vessels: list[Vessel], overrides: list[tuple]) -> list:
    """Lock, ban and deadline overrides as bounds on x; return what undoes them."""
    # TODO: set the bounds each override needs, and record what you change.
    return []


def undo_overrides(changes: list) -> None:
    """Put back every bound that `apply_overrides` changed."""
    # TODO: restore the recorded bounds.
    return None


def build(vessels: list[Vessel]) -> tuple[mathopt.Model, dict]:
    model = mathopt.Model(name="dry-docks")
    x = {(v.vid, t): model.add_binary_variable(name=f"x_{v.vid}_{t}") for v in vessels for t in v.years}
    for v in vessels:
        model.add_linear_constraint(sum(x[v.vid, t] for t in v.years) <= 1, name=f"once_{v.vid}")
    return model, x


if __name__ == "__main__":
    vessels = [Vessel("ISLA", (2027, 2028, 2029))]
    model, x = build(vessels)
    changes = apply_overrides(x, vessels, [("by", "ISLA", 2028)])
    print(x["ISLA", 2029].upper_bound)
    undo_overrides(changes)
    print(x["ISLA", 2029].upper_bound)

cases.says: a locked vessel docking in its year is allowed, and in another year or not at all is refused
a banned vessel that docks is refused
a vessel docking after its deadline is refused, and one not docked at all is allowed
a vessel docking in its deadline year is allowed
undoing the overrides restores each bound it changed, including one that was not 0 and 1
a lock on a year the vessel cannot dock in keeps the vessel out of dock in every year

origin.section: An Override Is Data, and Restoring the Bounds Undoes It

concepts: an override on start variables changes their bounds, and only an override on a sum needs a row
an override records the bounds it changed so that restoring them undoes it
